abstract: Travel restrictions, border screening and quarantine were widely used during the COVID-19 pandemic to prevent or delay the spatial spread of SARS-CoV-2, yet their effectiveness varied greatly across jurisdictions. To investigate how the timing and combination of border control measures interact with pathogen introductions and local transmission, we formulate a coupled Exporter--Importer epidemic model in both deterministic (ordinary differential equations) and stochastic (continuous-time Markov chain and multitype branching process approximation) frameworks. The model distinguishes latently infected, detected infectious and undetected infectious individuals, and explicitly separates recently arrived travellers in an introduction layer from the destination community. We derive analytical expressions for the control and basic reproduction numbers, final epidemic sizes and probabilities of outbreak extinction, and complement them with stochastic simulations. We show that pre-departure screening in the Exporter alone cannot prevent outbreaks in an Importer community with reproduction number larger than unity because latently infected travellers cross borders undetected. Post-arrival quarantine and screening in the introduction layer, as well as travel interruptions, can substantially reduce the attack rate in the Importer, but only when implemented with high stringency and triggered early. Triggering border interventions based on local detections in the Importer almost always acts too late because silent introductions precede local case detection, whereas triggers informed by surveillance in the Exporter provide a wider window of action. Effective protection of the Importer ultimately requires combining proactive, Exporter-informed border measures with local public health interventions that keep the community reproduction number near or below one.
